title: Perez reflects on 'one of my best weekends'
excerpt:
Sergio Perez believes his performance in the Azerbaijan Grand Prix was "one of my best weekends" in Formula 1, despite failing to reach the points for Cadillac.

The streets of Baku have been a happy hunting ground for the Mexican, who took victories at the venue in 2021 and 2023 when driving for Red Bull, and Perez was hopeful of a strong result again last weekend.

Although Perez enjoyed his best practice outings of the season, the Cadillac driver ultimately fell short in Qualifying and could only manage P20, as well as receiving a three-place grid drop for impeding.

But in the race, Perez managed to stay in touch with the midfield runners on his way to P14 and his joint best result of the season.

"I think it's been one of my best weekends, best performance in Baku and I've had some good ones here," said Perez.

"I'm pretty pleased with that, I think I drove at a high level the whole weekend, especially in the race but we are simply a second, two seconds off the pace to compete with the others.

"We stayed the whole first stint with the Williams, with the Audi, helped by the overtake mode. But at the end, we just didn't have the straight-line speed, we are too draggy on the straights.

"Plenty of things we need to improve, but as we know, it's going to be a difficult end of the year."

Cadillac have still yet to score a point during their maiden season of F1, with Valtteri Bottas' P13 in China the team's best result so far.

While no major upgrades are expected before the end of the season, Perez hopes the team can improve in other areas in order to hit the ground running in 2027.

"I think we don't have anything coming to the car unfortunately but I think operationally and pushing the team to improve and get the maximum out of the weekends, I think we are heading in that direction," he said.

"We just have to keep pushing a lot harder as a team and things will come."

title: Who impressed our Power Rankings judges in Azerbaijan?
excerpt:
George Russell was the driver to beat throughout the Azerbaijan Grand Prix weekend, as he charged to pole position and bagged an important win. But who else impressed our Power Rankings judges at the Baku City Circuit? Check out the latest scores and overall leaderboard below...

How it works

Our five-judge panel assess each driver after every Grand Prix and score them out of 10 according to their performance across the weekend – taking machinery out of the equation

Our experts’ scores are then averaged out to produce a race score – with those scores then tallied up across the season on our overall Power Rankings Leaderboard (at the bottom of the page)

Russell was back to his best on the streets of Baku – leading the way in Thursday practice, taking pole position by a whopping eight tenths of a second, and converting that into victory despite intense pressure from Red Bull’s Max Verstappen in the closing stages. Unsurprisingly, our judges could not fault his weekend performance.

Verstappen cut a hugely frustrated figure after Qualifying in Azerbaijan, with apparent power unit/battery issues leaving him back in eighth on the grid – a few hours after he had topped final practice. However, race day marked a big step in the right direction for driver and team, as the Dutchman cut his way through the field for a well-earned P2 finish, and very nearly the victory.

Isack Hadjar spent six weeks on the sidelines after injuring his wrist while training over the summer break, but you would not have known it based on the showing he delivered in Baku. Having steadily built up speed throughout practice, he earned a fine fourth position during Qualifying, and turned that into a “first proper podium on pure pace” in F1.

Pierre Gasly was understandably heartbroken when he arrived in the media pen after Saturday’s race. Pushing to turn an impressive P7 on the grid into another strong points haul, the Frenchman was taken out of the action by Alpine team mate Franco Colapinto, meaning they both went home empty-handed. “I don’t think I really have words, and I don’t need the words now,” Gasly sighed.

Esteban Ocon arrived in Azerbaijan stating that he is a “free agent” for 2027, with the Frenchman’s stint at Haas looking set to come to an end. Starting 14th after being impacted by yellow flags in Qualifying, Ocon did his talking on the track in the race by charging to eighth – ahead of team mate Ollie Bearman, and only just being beaten to the line by Racing Bulls’ Arvid Lindblad.

Bearman had qualified a few spots ahead of Ocon in 11th – agonisingly close to Q3. He led Haas’ charge for most of the race, only to make contact with Kimi Antonelli at a Safety Car restart and open the door for his team mate to slip through. Still, P9 at the chequered flag marked a solid result, and ensured the squad got both cars in the points.

Lindblad experienced a rollercoaster weekend around the streets of the Azerbaijani capital. The F1 rookie put himself on the back foot with an FP2 crash for the second successive event, and subsequently placed 15th in Qualifying, after which he admitted to “trying to be too special”. Race day brought some more drama in the form of a collision with team mate Liam Lawson, but he nonetheless did well to cross the line in P7.

Charles Leclerc was left with mixed feelings after Qualifying in Baku. On the one hand, he was pleased to come away with P2, but on the other hand admitted to Russell’s pole advantage being much bigger than anticipated. In the race, he could do nothing to stop Piastri and the Red Bulls from slotting ahead, though reclaimed P4 when the McLaren man locked up into Turn 1 late on.

As mentioned above, Lawson had been the lead Racing Bulls driver in Azerbaijan on his return from Red Bull, only for Lindblad to tag him into a spin at the first Safety Car restart. “I love getting taken out by my team mate. That’s pretty sick,” he sarcastically commented on the radio afterwards. The New Zealander did what he could to make up lost ground, but ultimately had to settle for 12th.

Williams unleashed a raft of updates at the Baku City Circuit as they looked to breathe some life into their difficult 2026 season. It appeared to do the trick, with both drivers progressing to Q2 before Carlos Sainz pulled out a mighty lap and reached Q3. A post-session penalty for failing to adhere to yellow flags saw the Spaniard drop from ninth to 14th on the grid, but he made the most of the drama to come away with a morale-boosting point.

Sergio Perez was in a punchy mood after the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, describing it as “one of my best weekends” in the sport after “driving at a high level” from FP1 to the chequered flag. He comfortably headed Cadillac’s efforts with the latest Ferrari power unit, managing to mix it with some of the midfield runners and come away with a respectable P14 – even if several retirements played their part.

Missing out

Just missing out on the Baku Power Rankings list are Audi’s Nico Hulkenberg, who came within a second of scoring a point, and the aforementioned Piastri and Antonelli – the former’s score impacted by that late lock-up, and the latter’s by his Q1 accident.

title: Sainz and Albon evaluate Williams’ Baku upgrades
excerpt:
Carlos Sainz recovered from a grid penalty in Baku to score for the first time in 10 rounds, but the Spaniard believes that Williams “need more” from their upgrades if they “want to fight for points regularly”.

The Grove-based outfit have struggled with an overweight car and additional performance issues for most of the 2026 season, leading to their decision to focus resources on a significant package introduced at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

It seemed to have an immediate impact as they enjoyed their first Q3 appearance of the year with Sainz, although he was later penalised with a five-place grid drop after failing to slow for yellow flags.

Aided by retirements for drivers further ahead, he improved from P14 to P10 to add a point to Williams’ tally, but was left with mixed feelings from the weekend as a whole.

“I think [it’s] what we deserved this weekend, to get a point for the team after the effort of the upgrade and a great Qualifying yesterday,” Sainz said. “Some good management there at the end for the last 10-15 laps, getting myself back into contention.

“I’m very disappointed after what happened yesterday, the way that was managed, the way that was handled. I was very depressed, let’s say, going into today. I managed to get a point for the team which was the target.

“[There’s] optimism in terms of I think the package is going to allow us to get back into positions where we can have some fun and fight with the others. The reality is that to get points, we’re still going to need each other’s help or some people’s help.

“I think the package is good to see, but after what I saw today, I think we’re going to need more if we want to fight for points regularly.”

For his team mate Alex Albon, the race in Baku was one to leave in the past – he locked up and crashed into the wall, triggering a Safety Car that ultimately led to restart chaos that eliminated multiple drivers.

Reflecting on the error, Albon explained: “Unusual crash, unusual place. I’ve not fully understood – maybe I braked a little later than the last lap, had a tailwind. We don’t like that corner as well, so we generally front-lock there. My fault, but it happens.”

He was nevertheless satisfied with the early performance of the upgrades, which included a new floor and adjustments to the rear of the car, but agreed with Sainz that further improvements should be made.

“We probably need a bit more aero in the car,” he said. “Actually, this car was not bad. This track suited us, our pace was actually quite good throughout the race. In the two medium speed corners of the track – Turn 1 and the last corner – we were slow, which is going to make the rest of the year difficult.”

title: 'Less pressure on me than there is him' – Russell on title
excerpt:
George Russell won his third Grand Prix of the season with victory in Baku, the Mercedes man standing on the top step of the rostrum for the first time since Austria.

In doing so, he cut his team mate’s lead in the Drivers’ Championship, Kimi Antonelli now 66 points ahead in the standings.

Antonelli arrived in Azerbaijan with an 81-point advantage over Russell following his back-to-back victories in Monza and Madrid. That translated to over three race wins, meaning the Italian could DNF at all three Grands Prix of this triple-header and still head to Austin in the lead.

Russell was in dominant form in Baku, topping two of the practice sessions before taking pole by the biggest margin of the season. His championship hopes were then aided by Antonelli crashing in Q1, and thus only qualifying 16th.

It was arguably the first big mistake from Antonelli since China, and while the 20-year-old recovered to finish fifth, Russell’s win saw him gain 15 points on his rival.

“There’s much less pressure on me than there is him," said Russell. "As I said [Friday], he’s had an incredibly flawless season. [Qualifying] was probably his first mistake of this whole season in a proper session... and he still came home in P5.”

“I didn’t really consider myself in this fight for a number of races, purely because my performance wasn’t strong enough. Now I feel like if the season were to have started today, or since the summer break, you know, I feel very much I would have been able to fight.

“Now I’ve got this big deficit. It can change quick. So, I’m not chasing that. I’m chasing to win every race, and what will be, will be.”

Antonelli vows to take lessons from ‘worst weekend of the season’

Russell has admitted already this season that he is not quite getting on as well with the new generation of cars as his team mate, despite a strong start to the year with pole and the win in Australia.

When he then took pole for the Sprint in Shanghai and won that dash, it looked like he was justifying his pre-season tag as favourite for the title. But after China, Russell didn't make the podium for four rounds, and was not helped by a run to the summer break that included a DNF in Spa and only seventh in Hungary.

Last season after Round 15, Oscar Piastri led Lando Norris by 34 points in the standings, with Max Verstappen a staggering 104 points behind the Australian. And yet come Abu Dhabi, Norris won the title, finishing 13 points ahead of his team mate and just two points clear of Verstappen.

That was a 47-point swing from Piastri to Norris, and a 115-point swing from Piastri to Verstappen. In such light, Russell’s 66-point deficit does not look quite so insurmountable, especially considering the Briton’s current form.

Whether the pressure will start to tell on Antonelli remains to be seen. He drove a sensible, considered race in Baku to recover to fifth, not taking any risks and not scything his way through the field with the same swagger he managed in Monza.

But if his team mate keeps performing like he did in Azerbaijan, Antonelli might find things are only going to get harder form here on out.

title: Norris apologises to Colapinto for Baku post-race comments
excerpt:
Lando Norris has apologised to Franco Colapinto for comments he made immediately after the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, admitting “it was wrong of me” to do so.

Colapinto locked up and went too deep at Turn 1 during the first Safety Car restart at the Baku City Circuit, taking out both Alpine team mate Pierre Gasly and the McLaren of Norris.

The stewards subsequently gave Colapinto a 10-second time penalty, which was converted into a five-place grid drop for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, given that the Argentinian did not finish Saturday’s race.

Speaking in the media pen following his own retirement, Norris stated that there are “some drivers that shouldn’t be in F1”, while also suggesting Colapinto should be banned.

On Monday, with the dust settling on the situation, Norris took to social media to explain that he had directly apologised to Colapinto, and they “are still good friends”.

“Tough weekend overall in Baku and of course a disappointing and early end to the race,” read a statement posted by Norris on Instagram.

“After the race, I sent Franco a message apologising for the comments I made that I simply should not have said. I know better and emotions were running high but that is not an excuse, it was wrong of me.

“I’ve made mistakes of my own over the years and I know this is very much a part of racing and fighting on the limit.

“Me and Franco came to a good understanding, are still good friends and are both excited to get back racing this weekend.”

title: Vasseur offers Ferrari upgrade promise to frustrated Leclerc
excerpt:
Ferrari Team Principal Fred Vasseur has promised that the Maranello-based squad will bring developments to the SF-26 “soon” after Charles Leclerc cited a lack of recent development as a reason behind their poor form in Azerbaijan.

Baku specialist Leclerc qualified second, an outcome that even surprised the team given the straight-line speed deficit that has been apparent all season.

However, race day brought something of a reality check when he slipped down the order to P5 in the opening laps as he was unable to defend.

In the end, a mistake by Oscar Piastri allowed Leclerc to finish P4, having fallen off the lead battle at around a second a lap in the mini sprint that followed the last Safety Car interlude.

With Lewis Hamilton having to settle for P6, it was not a great outcome for a team that have won twice this year – especially at a track where Leclerc often shines.

It wasn’t just about a straight-line performance deficit, as Hamilton cited his struggles to get the tyres into the right temperature window as a major factor behind his disappointing weekend.

“Honestly, we were surprised to be on the first row, because it’s one is the most demanding on the engine, and we were not expecting to do so,” said Vasseur.

“But we knew even starting from the first row that the opening laps, or in case of restarting after a Safety Car and so on, it would be difficult, and it was. But overall, I think that we maximised what we can do in Baku with P4 and P6. For us, we can't be satisfied with P4 and P6, but in Baku I think it’s the maximum.”

Ferrari’s performance on the straights has been an issue all season, and the team have had to make compromises to compensate.

“The biggest limitation is that when you are in this situation and you want to defend, you go in a kind of negative spiral,” said Vasseur. “Perhaps to try to run a bit lower downforce than say optimum, because you need to defend, and you are losing lap time.

“We had a similar case in Monza. There the pace was decent. The quali position was decent, but we were losing one position per straight line in the opening laps.

“The next races are a bit less demanding than this one. Let’s try to be back. And there is also a kind of convergence on the chassis, you can improve much quicker than with the engine. There is a kind of convergence of performance on the chassis.”

Hinting at recent improvements by rivals, he added: “I think the advantage that we had on the chassis is smaller, or not there anymore.”

Regarding Leclerc’s call for much-needed upgrades, Vasseur insisted that the wait won’t be long.

“I won’t give you the date, but soon,” he said. “Now it’s like this that we are all bringing upgrades at different places. I think McLaren did something this weekend, and Merc it will probably be next weekend, with Malaysia and [Kuala Lumpur-based Title and Technical Partner] Petronas.

“We will do it as soon as possible. For sure, sometimes you do steps, but it’s not always paying off, because sometimes you have to fine tune. Now I think everybody is switching to the next year’s programme, because even if it’s into the continuity, we have some changes on the regulations, and we have to anticipate this.”

title: How Baku highlighted McLaren’s straight line weakness
excerpt:
For the third time this year after China and Canada, McLaren failed to score a point in Azerbaijan as they endured a painful afternoon.

The huge frustration was that Oscar Piastri had enjoyed his best showing thus far of a troubled 2026 season, and the Australian looked set to log a podium finish, having run second for much of the race.

However, a mistake in the closing laps saw him head down the Turn 1 escape road, and given that the field had been bunched up by the Safety Car, he tumbled out of the top 10 before he could resume.

Lando Norris meanwhile had a messy weekend, suffering with a PU issue that cost him a little performance on the straights relative to his team mate.

He was at least destined to pick up some consolation points before he became collateral damage after the Franco Colapinto/Pierre Gasly collision. Not only was the World Champion bundled out of the race, he also lost some of the upgraded parts that had been introduced in Baku.

“It's been a very frustrating Saturday,” said Team Principal Andrea Stella. “I think we had issues and some mistakes, but at the same time I think we paid some fundamental limitations of our package in this kind of circuit, because we were not fast enough in the corners.

“But at the same time, mainly we were not fast enough in the straights, and this continuously exposed our drivers to being attacked and having to spend their race pretty much watching the mirrors rather than thinking at how they can progress in the race.”

Stella stressed that Piastri had done a great job in the circumstances, and crucially he appeared to have got on top of the issues that have been hampering him with the 2026 car.

Azerbaijan mistake 'certainly took me by surprise' – Piastri

“Oscar did this sort of defensive race very well,” said Stella. “He was very precise. His race reminded me very much of what he did in 2024 to win the race, when he held [Charles] Leclerc behind for a long time.

“But unfortunately, after the pit stop and having gone on the medium tyres, which were performing worse than the soft tyres, he had a lock-up and his race finished there.

“It's a real shame for Oscar, because he deserved to have a go at fighting for the podium, and also because Oscar has been driving very well the entire weekend. And we know that Oscar was in a little bit of learning trajectory to adapt to the 2026 car, and it would have been good to be rewarded.”

Stella admitted that life was made even harder for Norris by the PU issue that had hindered him in Qualifying, and which didn’t go away.

“If we look at Lando's race and the fact that he gradually went backwards, there's a few reasons for that,” he said. “We occasionally saw the same problem during the race, but not as systematic as in Qualifying.

"It was a little bit intermittent, but definitely there's a significant opportunity on the topic of fuel injection that we saw occasionally also on Oscar's car during the race. So this is a topic that we should look at high priority.

“In addition to that, Lando was overtaken by [Max] Verstappen, that was a quicker car. Lando was struggling a bit with the medium tyres – I mentioned Verstappen because he was on medium tyres as well as Lando, but he was faster. But credit to Oscar, Oscar managed to keep Verstappen behind.

“On Lando's side, we were struggling a little bit with power unit deployment, and also Lando was having some inconsistencies in his driving. When he was overtaken by [Lewis] Hamilton, he had a lock-up, and he had a few mistakes that meant that cars behind were within range. And when they are within range, then we struggle to defend, which goes back to the point on top speed.”

Stella conceded that it was a tricky weekend for Norris: “I would say that for Lando, this was one of the most difficult events in general that he has experienced in 2026, something that we need to take away, looking at whatever can be improved.

“But I would say most of the opportunities lie on the team side, and on the car side, because we need to be able to offer our drivers a car that is more raceable and just more consistent in terms of predictability.”

‘Some drivers shouldn’t be in F1’ – Norris on Baku clash

The top speed equation is always a complicated one, and it’s never just about pure horsepower.

“We need to look, I think, as a team, as to why the car wasn't as competitive as it should be in these long straights,” said Stella. “And it is very apparent that it is not a single factor. Certainly, we have always talked quite openly and transparently that we need to improve the aerodynamic drag of the car.

“There are a few factors, which refer to our ratios for instance – we need to look whether we are on the right ratios to compete in circuits in which you have this sort of top speed.

“And at the same time, when we look at the data and we compare with [Mercedes], we see that our power unit was not optimised. I think, while for Qualifying we managed to exploit pretty much the most that was available in the power unit, there's a few items that we were not able to optimise, and we paid the price in the race. So there's some work to do on the power unit side.”

The Baku upgrade package, which targeted slow-corner performance, delivered encouraging results despite the team's disappointing weekend.

“We are happy," said Stella. "The data seems to confirm that there's no issues with the upgrades, so hopefully there will be more benefit at the coming races. This has been a great effort by the entire team."

He admitted some components may have been lost in the crash but was confident replacements would arrive in time.

“Unfortunately, I think a couple of parts will have been lost with the crash, which is another downside of having been involved in these sorts of situations. But luckily, there's some more new parts coming, so we should be okay for the coming races.”

Stella also confirmed McLaren's development focus has switched to next year's car, with only previously approved updates still due to reach the MCL40.

“There's a tail of parts that will land trackside, so we will see still some new parts coming to the MCL40. But at the moment, as we speak, all the efforts are already concentrated onto next year's car, and what we see coming trackside is the result of parts being released a few weeks ago.”

title: Citroen name new Formula E team principal after Cyril Blais tragedy
excerpt:
Citroën Racing has confirmed Beth Paretta as its new team principal for the 2026/27 Formula E season, with Fred Espinos joining as deputy team principal as the squad reveals its first Gen4 livery.

Paretta steps up after serving as managing director throughout the team's debut campaign last season.

Espinos arrives from Lola Yamaha ABT, where he was deputy team principal, having previously worked as sporting manager at ABT Sportsline.

The appointments come after the tragic death of Cyril Blais, who held the team principal role before his passing was mourned across the Formula E paddock.

The championship paid tribute to him during the Tokyo double-header last July, where Nick Cassidy claimed back-to-back podiums for the team in his memory.

Citroen stick to iconic colours with full focus on Gen4 era

Citroën has stuck with the red, white and blue identity that proved popular with fans last season, now reworked for the more dynamic Gen4 machinery.

The reveal follows the team's confirmation earlier this month that it is reuniting with TotalEnergies for the GEN4 era, extending a partnership between the two French companies that dates back to 1968.

Cassidy and Jean-Eric Vergne remain in place as Citroën's full-time drivers for the upcoming campaign. Between them, the pair have 23 wins in Formula E, making them one of the most experienced line-ups on the grid.

Cassidy delivered the team's maiden win in just its second race, at the 2026 Mexico City E-Prix, with both drivers taking podiums across the calendar.

However, it is now all eyes on Gen4, with Paretta recognising it as a significant step up for the championship.

"GEN4 is much more than an evolution of the previous car: it is faster, more powerful and technologically more advanced, and it will change the way we approach race weekends," she said.

"For Citroën Racing, success will be about making the most of that opportunity from the very beginning. We feel well prepared, we have the strength and expertise of Stellantis Motorsport behind us, and we have a brand that is fully committed to the programme. Our objective is to translate all of that into being competitive out of the gate with strong performance on track."

Espinos, who represented his former team on the Shanghai podium when Lucas di Grassi won earlier this year, described the move as the right challenge at the right time.

"I'm very proud to join the team at such an important stage in its development," he said. "This is a project that brings together many of the ingredients needed to succeed: a brand with a strong motorsport heritage, an experienced team, two top-level drivers and a clear ambition as we enter the GEN4 era.

"We have a lot of work ahead of us, but the objective is clear: to be ready from the very start of the season."

title: Liam Lawson handed staggering verdict over Racing Bulls future
excerpt:
Liam Lawson has been given an overwhelming vote of confidence going into the remainder of the F1 campaign.

Lawson has enjoyed a strong season so far with Racing Bulls, which has also included a three-race cameo with Red Bull after Isack Hadjar broke a wrist in training during the summer break.

The New Zealander has scored points in 10 of the 15 rounds, including highs of sixth in the Monaco, British and Spanish Grands Prix.

Racing Bulls, though, has yet to confirm its driver line-up for next season, in particular with Red Bull junior and F2 title challenger Nikola Tsolov pushing for a place on the F1 grid.

In a RacingNews365 poll, we asked whether Lawson had done enough to retain his seat.

[Article continues below]

Lawson did 'a very good job'

In one of the most comprehensive results we have seen, just under 95 per cent agreed that he deserved another year.

Just 2.5 per cent of voters felt another junior driver should be given a chance, while the remaining 2.5 per cent said the team should wait until the end of the season before making a call.

From the perspective of Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies and Racing Bulls counterpart Alan Permane, it is clear they feel Lawson has performed well this year, strongly pointing to the fact he will be handed a fresh deal for 2027.

"He's done a very good job," said Mekies recently on Lawson's short return to Red Bull. "I think we all know how difficult it is to jump to a different team, to a different car, and I think that he has done that to the best of what could have been our expectations.

"So, I think he did a very good job, again very different pictures compared to the first two races of 2025 when he was in the team, so we are thankful and happy with that."

Permane also pointed to Lawson's chemistry with team-mate Arvid Lindblad after he returned from his Red Bull cover duty.

"Much as we love Yuki [Tsunoda], and the whole team does, he's a very popular figure, it's good to have Liam back in his car, in the team, working very, very well with Arvid," said Permane. "Those two lift each other up through the weekend."

title: Engine guru confirms Max Verstappen was right: 'I already had this view'
excerpt:
The debate over the new engine generation shows no signs of abating anytime soon. While teams and the FIA are still fine-tuning the energy distribution, engine guru Mario Illien speaks out clearly in an interview with RacingNews365. His conclusion aligns almost perfectly with what Max Verstappen has been saying for months.

Max Verstappen made clear from the outset that he is not a fan of the current F1 power unit. Far from it.

Verstappen has at least garnered support for his critical point of view from renowned engine guru Mario Illien, the co-founder of Ilmor and the engineer behind years of Mercedes power units in F1.

Illien agrees with the four-time F1 champion that the balance between the combustion and electric in today's Formula 1 cars is wrong.

The Swiss engine designer, who has won numerous titles throughout his career, made his views clear in an exclusive interview with RacingNews365.

"I think there's just too much electric power in them," said Illien.

"I think the hybrid concept is fine, but not in this proportion. Racing with so much electric power shouldn't be a handicap. Moreover, it's very complex and very expensive, and it doesn't make the fans any more enthusiastic.

"It's not exciting on TV either when you see cars having to give up after just two-thirds of the straight. The driver's role becomes less important, and now software, and how you use it, is becoming more important than the racing itself."

[Article continues below]

Illien knows he and Verstappen are right

Verstappen has been one of the most outspoken critics of the current power unit era. During pre-season testing in Bahrain earlier this year, the Red Bull driver delivered a scathing verdict on the regulations, comparing the heavy energy management demands to racing in Formula E.

"As a driver, the feeling is not very Formula 1-like," Verstappen said at the time. "It feels a bit more like Formula E on steroids.

"As a pure driver, I enjoy driving flat out, and at the moment, you cannot drive like that. A lot is going on, a lot of what you do as a driver, in terms of inputs, which have a massive effect on the energy, and for me, that's just not Formula 1, and maybe it would be better to drive in Formula E, right, because that's all about energy efficiency and management."

When RacingNews365 pointed out that Illien's comments echo those remarks from Verstappen, the Swiss expert did not hesitate to agree.

"Yes," said Illien. "I already had this view before it all started. It was clear to me early on that this is how it would turn out."

[Article continues below]

The solution for F1?

The FIA is working on shifting the ratio between the internal combustion engine and electric power from the current 52/48 split to 58/42 next season, and 60/40 in 2028. Illien does not see that as a bad move, but stopped short of calling it a fix.

Asked whether that shift would be enough, he replied: "It will improve things a bit, that's for sure. But it won't solve the problem."

As for what the actual solution should be, Illien had no doubts. He said: "I think the ratio we had until last year was a good one; it worked.

"And no one really criticised it back then, because it was a sensible approach. I think it's good and useful to recover kinetic energy, that's also good for regular cars. But that kind of racing, I just miss it."

title: F1 driver ejected from car at 280 km/h in horrific crash - Throwback
excerpt:
F1 driver ejected from car at 280 km/h in horrific crash - Throwback

One of the most horrific non-fatal crashes in F1 history took place exactly 36 years ago today.

Thirty-six years ago today, on 28 September 1990, the life of Martin Donnelly changed forever.

The Northern Irish Team Lotus driver was regarded at the time as one of the biggest talents on the grid, backed by an impressive record in the junior categories.

Donnelly had built his reputation with victory in the prestigious Macau Grand Prix in 1987 and strong results in Formula 3000.

When he was handed a surprise call-up to replace an injured driver at Arrows during the 1989 French Grand Prix, he qualified comfortably ahead of his experienced team-mate Eddie Cheever.

The talent was obvious, and Donnelly had already signed a new multi-year deal for the following season.

Everything pointed towards a bright future in the top flight. Until one fateful Friday in Jerez.

On the brink of death

During qualifying for the Spanish Grand Prix, the front suspension on Donnelly's Lotus-Lamborghini 102 failed.

A bell-crank came loose and gave way through a fast corner, and Donnelly lost all control of the steering. The floor of the car scraped along the asphalt before it speared into the barrier at around 280 kilometres per hour.

The impact was so violent that the carbon-fibre chassis snapped clean in two, tearing open the monocoque.

Donnelly was thrown from the wreck, still strapped to his seat, and landed separately on the track. Marshals did not need to cut him free from the car, because there was simply no wreck left to free him from.

FIA doctor Sid Watkins was among the first on the scene and immediately cleared the unconscious Donnelly's blocked airways to prevent him from choking. He suffered severe brain and lung injuries, along with multiple serious fractures to both legs and his collarbone.

He was placed in an induced coma in hospital due to organ failure and underwent several complex operations on his legs. At one stage, doctors even feared amputation.

Inspiration for an F1 movie

His recovery took years, with lengthy rehabilitation and lasting damage to his legs. Nerve damage left him physically unable to withstand the heavy pedal loads of a Formula 1 car, ruling out any return to the top flight.

Donnelly stayed involved in the sport regardless, working as a driver coach, running a junior team and serving as an FIA race steward.

He made occasional returns behind the wheel too, including in Lotus brand cup racing and, as late as 2015, once more in the British Touring Car Championship.

The crash itself led directly to stricter crash tests and tougher structural requirements for F1 monocoques, a legacy that still shapes every car on the grid today.

The accident did not stay confined to the history books either. It formed the direct blueprint for the backstory of lead character Sonny Hayes in the feature film F1.

The crash is visually recreated in the film, complete with a replica yellow Lotus 102 and overalls carrying Donnelly's sponsor logos from the time.

Producer Lewis Hamilton and the filmmakers contacted Donnelly beforehand to secure his approval and involve him in the scene.

title: Red Bull 'hierarchy' noted behind Baku team order debate
excerpt:
Red Bull was placed in a difficult position during the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, but opted not to implement team orders.

Racing driver Alex Brundle has highlighted the "hierarchy" that exists at Red Bull as a key reason why its drivers did not swap positions during the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

In the early stages of the race, Isack Hadjar was running behind his team-mate Max Verstappen but appeared to have more pace on the soft compound compared to Verstappen's medium.

The subject of team orders was floated at the time, but ultimately Red Bull opted not to switch their drivers around.

Brundle, however, did not see it as an unreasonable request.

"It's an interesting interplay between the two of them," Brundle told the F1 Nation podcast.

"The medium tyre worked so much worse on the Red Bull than the soft tyre did.

"I don't think it made a huge amount of difference to their eventual finishing positions when you look how far Isack was behind at the end of the race.

"But honestly, there was definitely a period where on the pit wall, I would have switched them back."

[Article continues below]

'Reasonable' to ask Verstappen to pull over

Verstappen went on to finish the race in second place, crossing the line just under two-tenths of a second down on winner George Russell.

The Dutchman has raced for Red Bull since early 2016 and has since established himself as one of the most successful drivers in the sport's history.

Over the last handful of years, he has faced no challenge from his team-mates and has consolidated his position as the team leader.

Brundle suggested that Red Bull did not wish to disrupt that stance by opting not to order a swap around of their drivers.

"Giving Isack a chance to overtake the McLaren was a reasonable thing to do, but it's still the Red Bull second seat.

"There's a hierarchy in that team, and they decided not to break it."

title: F1 fans split over Franco Colapinto penalty severity
excerpt:
Franco Colapinto's Azerbaijan Grand Prix ended in disaster on lap 36, when the Alpine driver locked his brakes into Turn 1 during a safety car restart and ran deep on the inside line, colliding with team-mate Pierre Gasly.

The impact pitched Gasly into the path of McLaren's Lando Norris, and all three cars were retired on the spot.

The stewards handed Colapinto a 10-second time penalty for causing the collision. Because the Argentine had already retired and could not serve it during the race, the sanction was converted into a five-place grid penalty for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

The stewards found Colapinto wholly or predominantly at fault, ruling that standard restart leniency did not apply since no other driver contributed to the incident. No penalty points were added to his Super Licence.

RacingNews365 asked its readers whether Colapinto had been given a fair penalty for the Baku incident.

Almost 36 per cent of respondents believe the sanction was appropriate.

But the largest share of voters, almost 46 per cent, felt the Alpine driver should have faced something harsher. Within that group, 29 per cent thought a race ban would have been the correct call, while the remainder simply wanted a stiffer punishment than the five-place grid drop.

The remaining 18 per cent went the other way, arguing the penalty was too severe given the circumstances of the restart.

title: Aston Martin reveal upgrade picture for final 2026 stint
excerpt:
Aston Martin has endured a challenging campaign this year, languishing towards the rear of the F1 field.

Aston Martin chief trackside officer Mike Krack has confirmed that there will be no more major upgrades fitted to the AMR26 package this year.

The Silverstone-based squad has endured a highly challenging campaign, languishing towards the rear of the field.

It has scored just three points across the season and only sits above newcomer Cadillac in the constructors' championship as the year enters its final stretch.

Aston Martin brought a major upgrade package to Hungary earlier this year, which is set to serve as its only big update.

"Enrico [Cardile, chief technical officer] made it quite clear that we will not bring a big upgrade package anymore," Krack told media including RacingNews365.

"But if there are insights in the wind tunnel, where we can do small steps, like we have done for Monza.

"Some small changes on the floor or on the bargeboards - these kind of things.

"We will continue to do these things, but I don't think that we will have a big, big package anymore.”

[Article continues below]

Krack details comparison challenges

While the Budapest upgrade offered Aston Martin a step forward in performance, it has continued to face woes, with that event in Hungary being the last time both of its cars saw the chequered flag.

Krack highlighted that there is an ever-moving goalpost in F1, making comparisons to other teams so difficult.

"At the end of the day, the track is just validating your tests that you do at home on the rigs and the simulations,” he said.

"So all of this is working. Sometimes you think you are less competitive or more competitive, and you often relate it directly to new parts or old parts.

"But you must not forget that the one you compare to is also changing. Other people are changing their cars.

"So you compare to them, and you do not really always know - 'have they improved or are we going slower?'

"Doing that exercise takes quite a lot of time. It's done at the factory, not at the racetrack. So you need to always carefully analyse."

title: Why Rafael Camara to Haas could spell disaster for Oliver Bearman
excerpt:
Rafael Camara's rise towards a 2027 Haas seat threatens to complicate would-be team-mate Oliver Bearman's path to Ferrari.

The American-owned outfit is working through its evaluation of Esteban Ocon's potential replacement, with the Frenchman having confirmed at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix that he is in the shop window for next season.

"At the moment, I'm definitely a free agent for next year," Ocon said in Baku. "There are things in discussions that are out of my control. There are certain topics that are out of my control. I will keep pushing until the end of the year and see how it goes."

Asked if staying with Haas remains an option for him, the one-time grand prix winner replied: "Let's see."

The current favourite to step into that vacancy, if Ocon leaving does transpire, is Camara, the 2025 F3 champion who leads this year's F2 standings with Invicta Racing.

With one hand on a second successive support paddock championship, the Brazilian is now in direct competition with Haas reserve driver Jack Doohan, as Leonardo Fornaroli and Ryo Hirakawa have been ruled out as Ocon alternatives.

And Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu has confirmed the selection process is all but complete.

"Soon, within the next couple of weeks," he said of a decision. "We've done all the evaluations. So just waiting to summarise our findings, have a discussion internally, have a chat with Gene [Haas], and then take the final decision."

Notably, Komatsu also stopped short of categorically confirming that Bearman himself will remain at Haas for 2027, a detail that has not gone unnoticed given the swirl of speculation around the Briton's future.

[Article continues below]

Two academy drivers, one cockpit

Bearman and Camara are not strangers. Both 21 years of age, they joined the Ferrari Driver Academy together in late 2021, plucked from the FDA Scouting World Finals in Maranello, and have since taken parallel routes through the junior single-seater ladder.

Bearman's, though, moved far quicker, with a F1 seat at Haas arriving in 2025 after his eye-catching Jeddah substitute drive for Ferrari the year before.

Camara has openly credited that trajectory as inspiration. "For sure, it's exciting," he told Sky Sports F1. "Also to see Ollie, from the Academy, and he had the opportunity to go to F1. It gives me the motivation to keep working, to keep improving myself, and hopefully one day maybe I can get also another opportunity."

Flattering as that sentiment is, it also frames the uncomfortable reality Bearman now faces. Should Camara land the Haas seat vacated by Ocon, Ferrari's junior pathway, the same one that funnelled Charles Leclerc — albeit only in free practice outings — and Mick Schumacher through Haas machinery before him, would suddenly house two of its own prospects in identical cars.

Whoever comes out on top in that fight would surely become the flag-bearer for a seat at the Scuderia once Lewis Hamilton eventually decides to walk away from F1.

Komatsu, meanwhile, insists the arrangement causes him no discomfort. "It doesn't really matter to me at all," the Haas boss said.

"We really want two fast drivers because that's the best way to grow this team. It doesn't matter if it's two Ferrari drivers or two Toyota drivers or two McLaren drivers... Honestly, it doesn't matter. Whoever is the fastest, that's the best one."

© XPBimages

The Aston Martin sidebar

Notably, Komatsu also stopped short of categorically confirming that Bearman himself will remain at Haas for 2027, a detail that has not gone unnoticed given the swirl of speculation around the Briton's future.

There has been chatter in recent months about contact between Bearman's father and Aston Martin, with the elder Bearman reportedly spotted on a couple of occasions around the team's operation.

The suspicion in the paddock is that this is being used as leverage tied to Fernando Alonso's situation at Aston Martin: for as long as Alonso's own future is not formally locked down, Bearman's camp can appear to be flirting with the idea of an alternative home.

The reading of that manoeuvre is that it is designed to pressure Ferrari into guaranteeing Bearman an unshakeable priority claim on a 2028 seat, with the implicit threat being that he could walk away from the Ferrari pathway altogether if that assurance is not forthcoming.

That, in turn, may explain why Komatsu was unwilling to give Bearman a categorical confirmation for 2027 at this stage.

Driver

Oliver Bearman

British

87

Bearman can't afford to stand still

But assuming he stays put at Haas, Komatsu's allegiance agnostic stance could be precisely the problem for Bearman, as it does not rule Camara out on account of their shared ties.

And a straight team-mate battle against a highly-rated academy stablemate, rather than an established outsider like Ocon, raises the stakes significantly.

Outperform Camara convincingly and Bearman strengthens his Ferrari case. Get beaten by him, or not handsomely enough, and the narrative shifts: the heir apparent usurped by the rookie just through the door.

Bearman has been careful not to sound complacent about his position. "Ferrari is the dream team," he said. "My goal remains to be a Ferrari driver one day. But I don't want to be sitting around for three, four, five years waiting for a seat."

He has also had to field questions over Red Bull's reported interest, after Sky Sports F1's David Croft revealed in July that the Milton Keynes-based squad is monitoring him as a long-term option should Max Verstappen ever depart.

Bearman played it down at the time, and the four-time F1 drivers' champion has since extended his stay until 2030, but it is good to know there are options out there.

"It's quite flattering to hear things like that, with a team like Red Bull who are incredibly successful, and to be connected with them in any way, even if it's just rumours, is very nice," Bearman said at the time. "But, as I said, it's just rumours, and I'm fully focused on what I'm doing here with Haas at the moment."

On his immediate prospects, the 21-year-old has been candid about the uncertainty. "Regarding my future, there is no conversation," he said. "I just drive the car. I think the rest will sort itself out if I perform at a good level."

That lack of clarity, paired with Charles Leclerc's long-term extension and Hamilton's continued competitiveness, already left Bearman with a narrow window at Maranello.

Adding an internal rival with Camara's pedigree at Haas, which Ferrari has actively financed through TPC mileage, only tightens it further.

© XPBimages

The Doohan alternative

There is, however, a scenario that would ease the pressure.

Jack Doohan, Haas's reserve driver since leaving Alpine, has already completed TPC running at Jerez alongside Ryo Hirakawa and Sho Tsuboi — neither of whom are in contention for the seat — as part of the same evaluation programme.

Handing the Australian the Ocon vacancy would keep Ferrari's junior queue exactly as it stands, with Bearman as the sole representative in a race seat and no immediate internal threat to his development.

Much of the paddock already treats the outcome as settled, with Camara assumed to be a done deal. Yet Komatsu was not being disingenuous when he said the decision has not actually been made.

Part of what is happening is that Ferrari's own lobbying effort is helping spread the impression that the matter is already concluded, even as Haas insists the final call is still to come.

But given the Scuderia's commercial and technical grip on Haas, through engine supply, gearboxes and listed components, two Ferrari juniors in the team is an outcome that cannot be ruled out.

And with Camara supposedly topping the evaluation shortlist and Ferrari team principal Fred Vasseur understood to be personally backing his preparation, the more convenient option for Bearman may not be the one Haas ultimately takes.

title: Alex Albon highlights bizarre 'three-wheel' issue behind race-ending Baku crash
excerpt:
Alexander Albon has offered an insight into his crash into the barrier at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix on lap 30, which brought an early end to his race.

The Williams driver had qualified 13th and was working his way through the field when the incident occurred, marking his third non-finish of the year.

The crash came at a track known for its long straights and heavy braking zones, where a gust of wind proved decisive in catching Albon out under braking.

But reflecting on the moment, Albon said the footage did not tell the full story of what happened in the cockpit.

"It was odd,” Albon told media including RacingNews365. “You see the rear cameras, so you don't really see the crash itself.

“I braked a little bit later, and then we had a big wind gust. I thought I would run a little bit wide, but I never thought I would hit the wall.

"It was weird. We'll look at the data. I'm sure I have to hold my hand up in that situation, but at the same time, we've had these issues before.

"We know our car likes to lift the front wheel, and sometimes when it does that, the penalty for front locking is huge on our car."

Williams car 'can't take' certain conditions

The issue Albon referenced, known in the paddock as three-wheeling, sees the inside front tyre unload or lift completely off the track under braking and cornering loads.

It has dogged the FW48 since pre-season, with Williams struggling to find a fix despite various setup changes across the year.

Albon expanded on how a simple decision to brake later did not comply with what the car could take.

"We know we three-wheel,” he said. “We know if brake a bit late, we can expose ourselves to that free-wheeling.

"With the wind gust, it tips it over the edge.

"It wasn't a huge amount. It was a few metres, but that's too much. We can't take that."

title: George Russell assigns 'pressure' label to Kimi Antonelli in F1 title fight
excerpt:
George Russell managed to eat into Kimi Antonelli's championship lead last weekend after claiming a third grand prix win of the season.

George Russell has asserted there is more pressure on the shoulders of Kimi Antonelli compared to his own as the F1 season enters its closing stages.

Antonelli remains the heavy favourite to seal his maiden championship this year as he sits on a lead of 66 points over Russell in the drivers' standings.

However, that gap was at 81 points before last Saturday's grand prix in Azerbaijan, with Antonelli's weekend hindered by a crash in qualifying that caused him to start from towards the back of the grid.

While Antonelli rose to fifth place, Russell claimed his third race victory of the season to eat into the championship deficit.

When asked by media including RacingNews365 if he feels he has less of a target on his back compared to Antonelli, Russell said: "Yeah, for sure.

"There's much less pressure on me than there is him. He's had an incredibly flawless season.

"[Friday] was probably his first mistake of this whole season in a proper session, qualifying, race, and he still came home in P5 [in the race]."

[Article continues below]

Driver

George Russell

British

63

Russell 'didn't consider myself' a factor in title fight

Russell began the campaign in strong form with a convincing victory at the season-opening round in Australia.

However, since then, Russell has failed to consistently match his team-mate, leaving him to concede that he was an outside bet in the title battle.

"I didn't really consider myself in this fight for a number of races, purely because my performance wasn't strong enough.

"I feel like if the season were to have started today, or since the summer break, I feel very much I would have been able to fight.

"Now I've got this big deficit. It can change quick. So I'm not chasing that. I'm chasing to win every race, and what will be, will be."

title: Charles Leclerc calls for Ferrari action after latest worry
excerpt:
Ferrari has failed to appear on the podium at the last five grands prix.

Charles Leclerc has insisted Ferrari “must react” to recent upgrades installed on the cars of rival teams.

Last time out at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, McLaren and Red Bull brought notable upgrades to their challengers as they sought to take a step forward in performance.

Ferrari, meanwhile, was without an upgrade in Baku and endured its fifth consecutive grand prix without an appearance on the podium.

While Leclerc acknowledged that the layout of the track isn't best suited to the SF26's characteristics, he admitted that its rivals have made a jump forward.

“I don't think this track particularly suits our car,” Leclerc told media including RacingNews365.

“But it's also true to say that McLaren and Red Bull did a step forward with the upgrades they are bringing, and that they have brought recently.

“They did a step forward that we didn't do, and we must react because losing some pace now is going to be very difficult to then take it back.

“Hopefully we can react very soon.”

Ferrari has 'a few things coming' to F1 car

Ferrari currently sit second in the constructors' championship, 72 points ahead of McLaren, who endured a miserable race in Baku, finishing outside the points.

But with Leclerc wary of the threat that is posed to Ferrari's runner-up position, he confirmed that it has more upgrades in the pipeline.

“We've got a few things coming,” he said.

“Whether it's going to be enough to close the gap, not knowing what the others have in store as well, is another matter.

“But we've got few things that shall help us do some steps forward.”

title: Should Ferrari appoint Christian Horner as its next team principal?
excerpt:
Christian Horner recently made no secret of his interest in Ferrari, claiming he would waive his demand for an ownership stake for one team and one team only - the Scuderia!

"I did 21 years sitting on the pit wall. I don't need to go back to that," Horner said in an interview with The Times. "At this stage in my life, there's only one team for which I would accept non-participation in ownership."

As to the team, in particular, he added: "Would I consider Ferrari? I mean, Ferrari is the biggest brand in Formula 1. It's the dream. And arguably it's the sleeping giant of Formula 1."

The 52-year-old, who left Red Bull last September after a negotiated settlement after being axed two months previously, is a free agent, believing "there's another dance" in him where F1 is concerned.

[Article continues below]

But is Ferrari the right move if the team opts to get rid of Vasseur, whose own contract is understood to run to the end of 2027?

Speculation was rife in the Baku paddock over the Azerbaijan Grand Prix weekend, with Vasseur addressing the Horner rumours after the race.

"Mr. Horner is looking for a job, everybody knows, everywhere," said Vasseur. "But what can I do? Just to try to do my best to push the team, to ask them to be motivated, focus on what is better today, and not to spend time with gossip."

It is clear, however, that Vasseur is growing annoyed by questions about his future, with speculation that he could be out at the end of the season after another disappointing campaign for the Maranello squad.

"We are not working in perfect serenity, if that is the question for me first and for everybody in the team, for the media," he said. "Fifty per cent of the questions are about this, and that is a bit of a frustrating situation."

Horner achieved remarkable success at Red Bull over his two decades at the helm, but would he really be a good fit?

title: Lando Norris issues apology to Franco Colapinto over 'emotional' comments
excerpt:
It takes a big man to do what Lando Norris has done!

Lando Norris has apologised to Franco Colapinto for the comments he made in the aftermath of their Azerbaijan Grand Prix crash, conceding his remarks calling for a race ban were "wrong."

Norris was among three cars eliminated at Turn 1 in Baku when Colapinto locked up on a lap 35 restart, clattering into Alpine team-mate Pierre Gasly, who was then sent into Norris on the outside line. All three retired on the spot.

Norris did not hide his frustration in the immediate aftermath, stating that such incidents deserved at least a one-race suspension, whilst also claiming there are some drivers who do not deserve to be in F1.

"If you cause a crash on a restart like this, you should have at least a one-race ban," said Norris.

"It is just careless from people. It costs a lot of money, all my parts are in the bin now and people should get banned. It is not driving that deserves to be in Formula 1."

Colapinto was handed a 10-second penalty by the stewards, converted into a five-place grid drop for this weekend's Bahrain GP in Malaysia. He immediately took responsibility for the incident by apologising to both Gasly and Norris.

[Article continues below]

Norris reflects and reaches out

But with tempers cooling and Norris himself facing online abuse over his comments, an issue Alpine publicly condemned, the Briton chose to reach out to the Argentine directly.

Posting on Instagram, Norris explained he had privately apologised to Colapinto before going public with his change of heart.

"Tough weekend overall in Baku and of course a disappointing and early end to the race," he said.

"After the race, I sent Franco a message apologising for the comments I made that I simply should not have said.

"I know better, and emotions were running high, but that is not an excuse; it was wrong of me. I've made mistakes of my own over the years, and I know this is very much a part of racing and fighting on the limit.

"Me and Franco came to a good understanding, are still good friends and are both excited to get back racing this weekend."

The exchange comes after several drivers, including George Russell and Max Verstappen, pushed back on Norris' original demand for a ban, with Russell calling it "too harsh" for what he described as a small error with big consequences.

title: Franco Colapinto compared to Max Verstappen in major mistake defence
excerpt:
Franco Colapinto has a former F1 driver firmly in his corner following the Azerbaijan GP.

Franco Colapinto has been compared to Max Verstappen by Juan Pablo Montoya, who defended the Argentine's costly restart crash at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix by arguing it stemmed from the same aggressive instincts that define the four-time world champion.

Colapinto was handed a five-place grid penalty for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia after stewards ruled him predominantly responsible for a multi-car collision at Turn 1 on the lap 36 restart in Baku.

The Alpine driver carried too much speed into the corner, locked his brakes and hit team-mate Pierre Gasly, who was then pushed into Lando Norris, eliminating all three cars.

Stewards rejected the usual leniency given for first-corner incidents, saying no other driver had contributed to the error, and converted his 10-second time penalty into the grid drop since his car had already retired with terminal damage.

Speaking to F1TV after the race, Montoya said he understood why Colapinto had gone for the gap.

"The difficult thing in that case is that you're aggressive, you see an opportunity and you have to admire it," Montoya said.

"I admire people who try. When you have a reset, they see it as an opportunity. Some people see a reset as 'I don't want to lose a position,' and Franco is the guy who wants to go and take advantage of it.

"When you're always the guy, like Max (Verstappen), who always sees an opportunity to take advantage of it, you're going to make mistakes."

Franco Colapinto 'almost' avoided triggering crash chaos

The former F1 driver pointed to the mechanics of the restart itself as a key factor behind Colapinto's misjudgement, with the long line of cars bunching up after a slow Safety Car period before accelerating hard down to Turn 1.

Assessing Colapinto's mistake, Montoya explained: "It's difficult because it seemed like everyone was braking very early.

"I think the issue is that, when you have a reference point and you're coming in, I don't know, at 320, 330 kilometres per hour and you brake at the 120-metre reference point, you expect that, coming in at 200, you're going to brake at the 80-metre one, and I think he expected everyone to go much further."

He continued: "The problem is, when you're that far back, you know, it's like a traffic jam: everyone's accelerating and accelerating, and you see him brake and he's going to hit someone, so he moves off and goes to the inside.

"He almost stopped the car. Yeah, he made a mistake and hit his teammate and took Lando out too. I mean, he made a mistake, but it was close."
